prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1-2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges). Monitor potassium and glucose during the steroid pulse (thiazide, salbutamol).

Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no tumour: in a 62-year-old former heavy smoker, repeat tumour screening during follow-up if the course is refractory or the disease relapses.
Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.
Admit to a neurology ward with seizure precautions, continuous cardiac monitoring and fall precautions for orthostatic hypotension.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide.

Treat the moderate hyponatraemia (128 mEq/L): stop the co-amilozide (thiazide) and review citalopram, assess volume status given the orthostatic hypotension (cautious isotonic saline if hypovolaemic, fluid restriction if SIADH), and correct by no more than 10 mmol/L in 24 hours.
Treat agitation and insomnia with low-dose benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioural management.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.

Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology; in this 62-year-old, a 3-month decline with focal seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, dysautonomia and inflammatory CSF is not a neurodegenerative presentation, and the scan would not change management.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) or other viral encephalitis
differential.key_features: CSF HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV and enterovirus PCR negative on an LP months into the illness; afebrile; MRI without haemorrhage or restricted diffusion; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Other antibody-mediated encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA receptor or DPPX)
differential.key_features: LGI1 encephalitis is the usual cause of limbic encephalitis with hyponatraemia at this age, but the serum neuronal-surface panel is negative (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, DPPX) and there are no faciobrachial dystonic seizures.
Raised by her 50 pack-year smoking history, but the onconeural antibodies are negative and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no tumour.
No periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG, no cortical or deep grey matter diffusion restriction, focal seizures and CSF inflammation with a positive CSF anti-GluN1.
A 3-month decline with focal seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic dysfunction and lymphocytic CSF is too fast and too inflammatory for a neurodegenerative dementia.
Sodium 128 mEq/L on co-amilozide and citalopram contributes to confusion but does not explain focal seizures, dyskinesias, CSF pleocytosis or the antibody.
Orthostatic hypotension on a diuretic can explain the collapse, but the ECG is normal (QTc 432 ms) and syncope does not explain the memory decline, staring spells or dyskinesias.
Stable citalopram dose, no clonus or hyperthermia (37.2 °C), CK 98 U/L; seizures, dyskinesias and CSF inflammation are not explained by depression.

key_clinical_evidence: Onset over 3 months of memory and behavioural change, word-finding and paraphasic errors, focal seizures with lip automatisms and orofacial dyskinesias: 4 of the six Graus 2016 groups, with orthostatic hypotension a possible fifth (autonomic) that her diuretic confounds.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titre 1:64) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive at a low titre (1:40) is read with the CSF.
MRI subtle left hippocampal FLAIR signal without restricted diffusion; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes.
EEG diffuse slowing, FIRDA and left temporal seizures, without periodic sharp-wave complexes; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
At 62, tumours are mostly carcinomas (Titulaer late-onset 2013): CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows none, and screening is repeated if the course is refractory.
Sodium 128 mEq/L on a thiazide and citalopram is worked up and corrected separately; earlier immunotherapy is associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A course under 3 months with focal seizures, orofacial dyskinesias and autonomic dysfunction is neither neurodegenerative nor depressive; it needs EEG, CSF and antibody testing.
red_herrings.data_point: Three months of memory decline with irritability and emotional lability in a 62-year-old with treated depression.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a neurodegenerative dementia or depressive pseudodementia and delays the encephalitis work-up.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatraemia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis. Here the thiazide and citalopram are plausible contributors.
red_herrings.data_point: Moderate hyponatraemia (sodium 128 mEq/L) on a thiazide and an SSRI.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent to attribute the encephalopathy to drug-induced hyponatraemia.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The diuretic may explain the orthostatic drop, but staring spells with lip automatisms, dyskinesias and memory decline are not syncopal; autonomic dysfunction is itself one of the Graus 2016 groups.
red_herrings.data_point: Collapse with orthostatic hypotension (107/75 to 82/58 mmHg) on a diuretic.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a syncope work-up (cardiac monitoring, echocardiogram) instead of the encephalitis.

contraindications: Class warning: haloperidol and other high-potency D2 antagonists are associated with severe neuroleptic intolerance (rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis) in anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
interactions: Hydrochlorothiazide (co-amilozide) + citalopram: additive risk of hyponatraemia; thiazide-induced hypokalaemia (partly offset by the amiloride component) would add to the QT risk of citalopram.
Hydrochlorothiazide + methylprednisolone: additive potassium loss, partly offset by amiloride; salbutamol adds to it. Monitor potassium.
Citalopram: maximum 20 mg daily above the age of 60 (QT prolongation); avoid other QT-prolonging drugs.
IVIG: can lower the measured sodium (pseudohyponatraemia with indirect ion-selective electrodes); check serum osmolality before treating a fall. Risk of thrombosis and volume load in older patients.
Levetiracetam or lacosamide + current medicines: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; lacosamide prolongs the PR interval.
Aciclovir: no interaction with her medicines; maintain hydration (crystal nephropathy).
warnings: Methylprednisolone pulses: monitor glucose, blood pressure and potassium; steroid psychiatric effects can mimic the encephalitis.
Rituximab: screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc) before the first dose.
Penicillin allergy (rash): not relevant to the immunotherapy; consider it for any antibiotic.

patient.history_present_illness: This 62-year-old right-handed retired school administrator presents to the emergency department following a witnessed collapse at home with brief loss of consciousness lasting approximately 30 seconds. Her husband reports that she was standing in the kitchen when she suddenly became unresponsive and fell to the ground. There was no witnessed tonic-clonic activity, tongue biting, or urinary incontinence, though she was briefly confused upon regaining consciousness. She has no recollection of the event. More significantly, her family has become increasingly concerned about progressive deterioration in her short-term memory over the preceding three months. Initially, she began misplacing household items and forgetting recent conversations, which both she and her husband attributed to stress related to her recent retirement. Over the following weeks, she forgot appointments, repeated questions she had asked minutes earlier, and on one occasion left the front door wide open overnight. She has also exhibited uncharacteristic irritability, emotional lability, and intermittent episodes where she appears to 'zone out' for several seconds before resuming activity. Her husband reports at least three such episodes in the past two weeks, during which she stares blankly and makes subtle repetitive mouth movements. She has also complained of persistent insomnia over the past month despite no change in her citalopram dose. Over the most recent week, her confusion has worsened noticeably: she became lost on a familiar walk to the local shop, could not recall her grandchildren's names, and was found attempting to use the television remote to make a phone call. She has had no recent illness, fever, headache, or focal weakness. There is no history of recent travel, tick exposure, or new sexual contacts. She has no prior psychiatric hospitalization or psychotic episodes. Her extensive smoking history is noted but she quit two years ago after a health scare involving a persistent cough that resolved with cessation. She continues to use her inhalers as prescribed for mild residual symptoms.

neurological_exam.additional: Significant postural hypotension noted: blood pressure drops from 107/75 mmHg supine to 82/58 mmHg upon standing. Intermittent orofacial dyskinesias observed, including lip-pursing and subtle tongue protrusion movements. One brief episode of behavioral arrest lasting approximately 15 seconds witnessed during the examination, with staring and rhythmic lip movements, followed by brief confusion. Heart rate varies between 56 and 78 bpm during the encounter.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing shows mild bilateral dysmetria, though this is likely confounded by inattention. Heel-to-shin testing is grossly normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements are full without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact to light touch bilaterally. No facial asymmetry. Hearing is grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue is midline without fasciculations. Subtle intermittent lip-pursing movements noted during examination.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly unsteady with slight widening of base. Able to walk without assistance but requires supervision. Tandem gait is impaired.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but disoriented. Oriented to person only; unable to state the date, month, year, or hospital name. Speech is fluent but with intermittent word-finding difficulty and occasional paraphasic errors. She becomes easily frustrated when unable to answer questions and at times becomes tearful without clear provocation. Attention is impaired; unable to perform serial 7s or spell WORLD backward. Short-term memory is profoundly affected; recalls 0 of 3 objects at 5 minutes. Abbreviated mental test score 5/10. She intermittently stares blankly for several seconds before resuming interaction.
neurological_exam.motor: Tone is normal in all extremities. Strength is 5/5 throughout when patient cooperates, though effort is intermittently inconsistent. No pronator drift. No muscle wasting. Occasional involuntary jerking movements of the right hand noted.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally (brisk), Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch and pinprick in all extremities. Proprioception is intact at the great toes bilaterally. Detailed sensory examination limited by patient's fluctuating attention.
